newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa banks offer strong support to crime bills.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa banks offer strong support to crime bills.

text.p: The Council of South African Banks (Cosab) came out in strong support on Friday of draft legislation to bolster the fight against crime but warned against over-hasty drafting.
"We'd rather have good law two months later than have to spend years sorting out this legislation," Cosab general manager Stuart Grobler told parliament's justice committee.
The committee is holding hearings on the first of six laws designed to bolster the courts in the fight against organised crime and drug trafficking.
The package includes a Proceeds of Crime Bill, which obliges institutions and individuals to report any suspicion that property or money they handle could be criminal profits.

Grobler took issue with some evidence given earlier this week by the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), which opposed the suggested criminal liability to report a suspicion of crime rather than actual knowledge.
Questioned by co-chairman Mohseen Moosa, he also rejected the JSE's suggestion that institutions be allowed to regulate themselves on reporting proceeds of crime or money laundering.

"We don't believe you can self-regulate on this," he said. "I think we have been living with this idea longer. I think the JSE are experiencing something of a culture shock, but we are used to the idea."
Grobler said the draft needed to be fine-tuned to define what could be considered reason to suspect criminal profit and who should be required to report suspicion.
"The bill is not clear enough on what is the duty of care of front line staff like cashiers. They could face 15 years in prison if they get it wrong," he said.
- Removal of the attorney-client privilege on trust account dealings to prevent them being used for money laundering;
- Greater clarity on the order of claim on funds that emerge to be criminal proceeds and whether government has a right to seize proceeds of crime irrespective of prior claims;
- The Reserve Bank should have the right to freeze funds briefly to allow time for an enquiry without telling a suspect that he is under investigation for money laundering;
- A reporting office should be created to ensure that reported suspicions do not disappear "into a bottomless bureaucracy";
- A mechanism should be provided to clear those named in error within a limited period of time and clarity on whether a bank can continue to do business once a suspicion is established.
